item.title: Trooper texted ICE on Signal to detain a teen. Now DPS says it must stop
item.dc:creator: Kelly Wiley, Beth Peak
item.description: DPS emails show repeated warnings about messaging apps and preserving evidence after video captured a trooper’s Signal exchange with ICE about an 18-year-old.
item.content:encoded:
Body worn camera video showing a Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS) trooper used Signal to notify federal immigration authorities about an undocumented teenager last summer, prompted an agency-wide warning from a senior leader within DPS, email records show.

The 28-minute video from early May shows a quick hand-off: a trooper pulling over a high school senior who was on his way home from a night shift at an Austin fast food restaurant; the trooper sending federal immigration authorities a picture of the teen’s ID through encrypted messaging application Signal; U.S. Immigration and Customs officials responding “detain” in the Signal chat before showing up and taking the teen into custody.

Within five days of NBC Austin affiliate KXAN publishing the footage, DPS’ Deputy Director of Law Enforcement Operation sent chiefs an email saying, “it seems we are still experiencing issues with third-party messaging apps.”

Records show it was not the first time he raised concerns about apps, like Signal – that is known for allowing users to automatically delete messages, and issues properly preserving evidence, like conversations between law enforcement officials.

In an email to the DPS chiefs, Lt. Col. Jason Taylor explained body camera video showing a DPS commissioned officer using a third-party app, on his personal phone, to communicate with a federal agent opened the employee’s personal device to public information requests.

Taylor said officers should only utilize approved applications, and specifically, Bridge4PS as the primary messaging application. Taylor said the Bridge4PS platform was interoperable across multiple government agencies and “makes cutting and pasting discoverable (and open records) material easy from the app to a PDF.”

The Texas Department of Information Resources said it has a zero-dollar contract with the Houston-based company NP Strategies, LLC allowing multiple state agencies to use the Bridge4PS platform at a pre-negotiated price. DPS has not yet responded with how much it pays to use the technology under the state’s contract.

Lt. Col. Taylor also forwarded a 2024 email where he raised similar concerns with officers using third-party messaging apps, like WhatsApp and Signal, to group chat with other agencies during criminal investigations. The official warned that those messages must be submitted with the case file to prosecutors to comply with state law.

He wrote that many of the message threads involve multi-agency task forces or multi-agency operations – and that the agency was bound to submit the messages as evidence when applicable, even when others do not.

“If another agency submits these items as a part of their case packet and we fail to do so then it is pretty obvious we are not in compliance with statutory requirements,” Taylor said in the March 2024 email.

Texas DPS officials have not responded to emails and calls from KPRC 2’s ENOUGH team about the body camera video or the emails requesting officers stop using the messaging applications.

In September, the agency released to our team a redacted screenshot of the messages sent between the trooper, who was granted limited immigration authority as a 287(g) trained officer, and ICE agents on the night of the traffic stop.

The screenshot shows the conversation already able to be seen partially on body camera: the trooper sending a picture of what appears to be his Houston Independent School District student identification card, and a text saying, “18. Says he’s from Mexico,” Then the ICE agent responding with a picture of the teen’s information, including the unique federal identification number for immigrants, and the word “Detain.”

The screenshots also show part of another conversation where people whose names are redacted but identified with “ICE” next to message in the chat, texting “stand-by,” “release,” and “status check.” One of the photos that appears to come from the DPS trooper at 10:39 p.m. is also redacted.

Freedom of Information Foundation of Texas Board Member, and Houston trial lawyer, Tom Gregor said the preserved messages are somewhat promising and suggest some of the officers are abiding by the protocol the agency has put in place.

“The open question on that is whether all officers are doing the same thing,” Gregor said. “Really the ultimate question is what mechanisms are in place in the agency to make sure that these communications are being maintained because they are public record and it should not be simply trust, and hope that the officers and personnel are doing the preservation on their own.”

The teen in the video was released in time for graduation after his attorney quickly filed a habeas corpus petition seeking his release and U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Austin, pushed for it.

item.title: House fire on Terry Street damages neighboring homes in Houston
item.dc:creator: Katherine Levens, Ajay Patel
item.description: A house fire broke out early Oct. 18, 2026, on the 2800 block of Terry Street in Houston, prompting Houston Fire Department crews to respond at about 5:39 a.m.
item.content:encoded:
A house fire broke out early Sunday morning in Houston, spreading damage to at least two neighboring homes, according to the Houston Fire Department.

Houston Fire Department (HFD) crews responded to the 2800 block of Terry Street at approximately 5:30 a.m. on Oct. 18, 2026. Firefighters appeared to have the flames mostly under control by 6 a.m., roughly 20 minutes after crews arrived on scene.

  • Man drowns in Sims Bayou after swimming while stranded with broken-down car, Houston police say

HFD confirmed the home was vacant at the time of the fire, and no injuries were reported. Both homes neighboring the original structure also sustained damage from the blaze. Crews remained on scene until approximately 8:15 a.m. Investigators are still working to determine the cause of the fire.

A neighborhood staple

While no one was physically harmed, the fire carries a deep emotional toll for the family connected to the home.

Joycelyn Turk said her mom used to live there before she passed away, and that she grew up in the house.

“It’s a heartbreaking feeling,” Turk said.

Turk says she rushed over there in her pajamas when she was notified of the tragedy, HFD got called out there around 5:30 Sunday morning.

Family members described the house as a neighborhood staple for years. They recalled their grandmother, who once lived there, as someone who regularly cooked food for neighbors — and said the feeling was mutual, with others in the community doing the same and gathering together for neighborhood hangouts.

The home has sat vacant for the past few years, but its significance to the family has never faded. Family members said the loss of irreplaceable mementos inside the home is the hardest part of the situation — items that no insurance payout or rebuilding effort could ever restore.

Among those mementos: photo albums and pictures of Turk’s parents building the house from scratch.

“My mother and father, when they moved down here, they built the house from scratch. We have pictures of them on the roof, building the house. I’m pretty sure all that’s gone,” Turk said.

Prisess Allen, a family friend who lives one street behind the home, said she was first alerted to the fire through her Ring doorbell — but said seeing the destruction with her own eyes was a different story.

“It’s a hurting feeling that this happened to us,” Allen said.

Allen echoed the sentiment that the loss goes far beyond the physical structure.

“You can get a new house, but you can never get the memories you had in the house,” Allen said.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

item.title: Woman detained after shooting two men during altercation at Cypress Station apartment complex, deputies say
item.dc:creator: Katherine Levens
item.description: A verbal dispute between residents at The Park at Cumberland Apartments in Houston escalated into a physical altercation on Oct. 17, 2026, after which an adult woman fired into a nearby crowd, wounding two men.
item.content:encoded:
A verbal dispute between residents at a Houston apartment complex escalated into a shooting Saturday evening, leaving two men wounded, according to the Harris County Sheriff’s Office.

Harris County Sheriff’s deputies responded to a shooting call at The Park at Cumberland Apartments, located at 505 Cypress Station Drive, at approximately 7:48 p.m. on Oct. 17, 2026.

  • A fantastic fall feel in Houston this Sunday

Investigators say a verbal altercation between residents turned physical before an adult woman fired into a crowd of several people standing nearby. Deputies arrived to find two adult men with gunshot wounds.

EMS transported both men to a hospital, where they are expected to survive. Preliminary information indicates both wounded men were involved in the physical altercation prior to the shooting.

The woman was detained at the scene. Authorities say there is no ongoing threat to the community.

Detectives are interviewing witnesses and searching for surveillance video. Investigators have not yet determined the relationship between those involved.

Detectives will present the case to the Harris County District Attorney’s Office to determine whether charges will be filed.

media:content.media:description: Harris County Sheriff's on scene of a shooting at a apartment complex.

item.title: A fantastic fall feel in Houston this Sunday
item.dc:creator: Anthony Yanez
item.description: A gradual warm up is expected this week
item.content:encoded:
Sunday’s forecast:

After a cold start to the day afternoon high temperatures climb to the mid-70s under mostly sunny skies. Unlike the past two days northeast winds are light 5 to 10 mph.

Work week warm up:

High pressure will slowly build into the state of Texas this week. This will bring a gradual warm up to weather. The humidity remains low. While there are some days we’ll climb to near 90° there won’t be much of a heat index.

Tracking the tropics:

There is an area off the east coast that has a 30% chance of becoming our next tropical system. It will bring strong winds and coastal flooding along the coast but most likely will not make a direct hit on the United States.

Extended forecast:

This is a dry weather pattern. I don’t have a chance of rain in the next 10-days! I also don’t see a whole lot of humidity this week. While temperatures climb to near 90°, it will feel much closer to 90. Have a great week.

item.title: Man drowns in Sims Bayou after swimming while stranded with broken-down car, Houston police say
item.dc:creator: Katherine Levens
item.description: A man drowned in Sims Bayou near Houston’s Allendale neighborhood on Oct. 17, 2026, after entering the water fully clothed despite a bystander’s warning while his car was being repaired.
item.content:encoded:
A man drowned in Sims Bayou near the Allendale neighborhood of Houston Friday evening after going into the water despite warnings from a bystander, according to Houston Police Department officials.

The incident happened around 5:30 p.m. on Oct. 17, 2026, near Mosa Creek at Allendale.

According to Lt. Pulido with HPD, the victim’s car broke down in the area when a witness stopped to help him with repairs.

“While they worked on the car, the victim said he wanted to swim in the bayou, and the witness said he told him not to,” Pulido said.

Despite the warning, the victim entered the bayou fully clothed and began swimming.

  • ‘No Kings’ rallies draw demonstrators across Houston area ahead of early voting

“The victim then went under multiple times, and on his last attempt to go under, he never came back up,” Pulido said.

HPD responded to the scene and recovered the victim’s body.

item.title: Military service member hospitalized after fall during rappelling demonstration at UTSA football game in San Antonio
item.dc:creator: Brittany Taylor
item.description: A military service member was taken to a hospital after falling during a rappelling demonstration before a University of Texas at San Antonio football game Saturday night, according to reporting by KPRC 2’s sister station, KSAT.
item.content:encoded:
A military service member was taken to a hospital after falling during a rappelling demonstration before a University of Texas at San Antonio football game Saturday night, according to reporting by KPRC 2’s sister station, KSAT.

The incident happened just before 7 p.m. at the Alamodome in San Antonio, where UTSA was scheduled to face Navy, according to the San Antonio Fire Department, KSAT reported.

The service member was participating in a pregame demonstration with three other officers as part of UTSA’s Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans night, witnesses told KSAT. The service member’s condition was not immediately known.

Witness Adrian Corey told KSAT that the fall happened as the band began playing.

“Once the band started playing, there was a guy that fell down,” Corey told KSAT, describing the service member as coming down quickly.

Witnesses told KSAT that UTSA staff surrounded the service member as he received medical attention. Corey said the crowd fell silent and the band stopped performing.

“It was a very sad moment and we don’t know (his condition),” witness Siomara Corey told KSAT, adding that attendees had asked for prayers.

KSAT reported that it had reached out to UTSA and its athletics department for additional information but had not received a response at the time of its report.

Stay updated on this story with KSAT News.

item.title: ‘No Kings’ rallies draw demonstrators across Houston area ahead of early voting
item.dc:creator: Brittany Taylor, Joy Addison
item.description: “No Kings” rallies and voter-engagement events are taking place across the Houston area Saturday, with organizers encouraging residents to make a plan to vote ahead of the November election.
item.content:encoded:
Demonstrators gathered outside Houston City Hall on Saturday for a “No Kings” rally, joining a nationwide movement raising concerns about government accountability and encouraging voter participation ahead of the November election.

Other events were scheduled across the Houston area, including The Woodlands and west Harris County, as organizers urged eligible voters to make a plan to vote.

Participants at the Houston rally pointed to a range of concerns, including immigration enforcement, public education, property taxes, affordability and the direction of the country.

For Ashley Escandon, an organizer with 50501-Houston, the event was an opportunity to help people understand their voting rights and prepare to cast their ballots.

“We have the power to make change. We have the power to go out and vote. And we have the power for a better future,” Escandon said.

Demonstrators raise concerns about Texas and national politics

Some attendees said they were frustrated with the current administration and wanted to see changes in government.

Kathy Lamb said she attended the rally to encourage people to vote.

“The real way we can change things is to vote in this election,” Lamb said.

Other demonstrators highlighted issues affecting families across Texas, including public schools, property taxes and the rising cost of living.

Although attendees had different priorities, several emphasized voting as a way to influence decisions affecting their communities and the country.

More ‘No Kings’ events planned across the Houston area

Saturday’s Houston City Hall rally was among several events organized across the region as part of the nationwide “No Kings: Vote Early” effort.

Other gatherings included:

  • The Woodlands: Greater Woodlands Indivisible and the League of Women Voters of Montgomery County organized a voter-engagement event from 9 to 11 a.m. at the intersection of Lake Woodlands Drive and Six Pines Drive.
  • West Harris County: “Women of the West: No Kings. Just Queens.” was scheduled from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. at the Steve Radack Community Center, 18650 Clay Road. Organized by Harris County Democratic Precinct 0463 Chair Dave Romero, the event brought together women candidates running for Congress and the Texas House.
  • Houston City Hall: A rally and march was scheduled from 4 to 6 p.m. at 901 Bagby St., with local grassroots organizations encouraging civic engagement and voter participation.

The Women of the West event featured Laura Jones, a candidate for U.S. Congressional District 8, along with Dr. Darlene Breaux, Stefanie Boyd and Sara McGee, candidates for Texas House districts 149, 126 and 132, respectively. Organizers said the gathering offered residents an opportunity to hear from candidates about public education, health care, infrastructure and flood mitigation.

Additional events were listed in communities including Cypress, Katy, La Porte, League City and Missouri City.

Organizers encourage voters to prepare

The “No Kings” movement organizes demonstrations around concerns about executive power and government accountability. Saturday’s “Vote Early” theme focused on turning that engagement into voter participation.

Escandon said organizers were sharing information and resources to help eligible voters understand their rights and voting options.

The broader voter-engagement effort is described as nonpartisan, although individual events may feature candidates or organizations with specific political affiliations.

Organizers also emphasize nonviolent participation, lawful conduct and de-escalation if disagreements arise.

item.title: Houston firefighters honor 85 members who died in the line of duty at annual memorial ceremony
item.dc:creator: Brittany Taylor
item.description: Houston firefighters, families and friends gathered Saturday to honor the 85 members who have died in the line of duty during the annual Houston Firefighters’ Memorial Ceremony.
item.content:encoded:
Houston firefighters, families and friends gathered Saturday to honor the 85 members who have died in the line of duty during the annual Houston Firefighters’ Memorial Ceremony.

The ceremony was held Oct. 17 at the Houston Firefighters’ Memorial Garden, located at the Houston Firefighters Relief and Retirement Fund facility in north Houston. The annual event honors fallen firefighters and remembers members who have died.

During the ceremony, special guests, including family members and elected officials, were selected to place a fire helmet and a rose in honor of the deceased.

The Houston Firefighters’ Memorial Garden was dedicated in March 2001. The memorial serves as a place to recognize the sacrifices of Houston firefighters who died in the line of duty and to honor their lasting legacy.

The annual ceremony brings together members of the fire service and the community to remember those who made the ultimate sacrifice while serving others.

item.title: 2 people shot on Aldine Bender Road, suspect on the run, HCSO says
item.dc:creator: Brittany Taylor
item.description: Two people were shot Saturday around noon in the 5600 block of Aldine Bender Road, according to the Harris County Sheriff’s Office.
item.content:encoded:
Two people were shot Saturday around noon in the 5600 block of Aldine Bender Road, according to the Harris County Sheriff’s Office.

Both victims were taken to a hospital with injuries that were not considered life-threatening, HCSO said.

The male suspect fled the scene and remained on the run as of Saturday afternoon.

The investigation is ongoing.

item.title: Man shot in neck at Houston nightclub now investigated as suspect
item.dc:creator: Ricky Munoz, Heikki Mustonen
item.description: Two people were shot in the neck in the parking lot of Houston’s Magnolia Club after an argument between two men escalated and both allegedly fired guns; both victims underwent surgery and are stable.
item.content:encoded:
Two people were shot in the neck outside a Houston nightclub early Saturday morning, and police say one of the victims is now being investigated as a possible suspect.

The shooting happened around 1:57 a.m. in the parking lot of the Magnolia Club, located in the 5000 block of Griggs Road.

Both victims, a man and a woman, had to have surgery. Houston police say both are expected to be okay.

But what the injured man told officers after getting to the hospital has now become a major part of the investigation.

  • 2-alarm warehouse fire at UniClean America prompts hazmat response in northwest Houston

How did the shooting start?

According to Houston Police Lt. Pulido, two men got into an argument in the club’s parking lot.

Police still don’t know what they were arguing about.

At some point, both men pulled out guns and started shooting at each other.

“It took place outside in the parking lot,” Pulido said. “They got into some sort of argument. We don’t know what the argument was about. And they both pulled out a firearm. And started shooting at each other.”

A man and woman were both shot in the neck.

Police say the two are friends, although investigators have not explained exactly how the woman became caught in the shooting.

How did one of the victims become a possible suspect?

When officers arrived at the club, they detained one man and found a gun.

Meanwhile, the two injured people were taken to a nearby hospital in the same vehicle, with police accompanying them.

But once officers got to the hospital, they learned something else.

The man who had been shot told police he had also fired his gun during the argument.

“When officers got to the hospital, they got a statement from one of the victims and the victim stated that he also shot back at the suspect,” Pulido said.

That statement led police to detain the injured man at the hospital as a possible suspect.

Investigators have not announced any charges or explained whether they believe the man acted in self-defense.

What happened to the two people who were shot?

Both victims were shot in the neck and underwent surgery.

Police say their conditions are stable and both are expected to be okay.

Their names and ages have not been released.

Investigators have not said whether the woman was involved in the argument or was simply nearby when the shooting happened.

  • Trooper texted ICE on Signal to detain a teen. Now DPS says it must stop

Are police still looking for someone?

There are still questions about exactly how many people were involved.

At the scene, Pulido said officers had detained both men believed to have fired guns.

However, initial information provided to KPRC 2 indicated police were still searching for another suspect.

KPRC 2 has requested clarification from the Houston Police Department about whether anyone else is being sought.

Police say there is no ongoing threat to the public.

Investigators are also working to determine what started the argument and the circumstances surrounding the shooting.

This is a developing story. Check back with Click2Houston.com for updates.

What do you think?

If someone is shot during an argument and tells police they fired back, what questions should investigators answer before determining whether the shooting was self-defense?

item.title: How to become a poll worker in the Houston area for 2026 midterm election
item.dc:creator: De'Anthony Taylor
item.description: Interested in working the Nov. 3 election? Find Houston-area poll-worker application links, eligibility information and questions to ask about pay and training.
item.content:encoded:
Houston-area residents interested in working the Nov. 3 election can start with their county’s election office to check eligibility, training, and available assignments.

Texas early voting runs Oct. 19-30. With voting approaching, prospective workers should ask whether their county can still place and train new applicants for this election. An application page does not guarantee an available position.

Who can become a poll worker?

The Texas Secretary of State lists U.S. citizenship and qualified-voter status in the jurisdiction conducting the election among the basic eligibility requirements. Please have your county confirm the requirements for the particular position.

Harris County’s November training page says adult vote-center workers must be registered voters in Harris County. It identifies high school students as an exception through the student-worker program.

SEE MORE: Texas election guide 2026 – Dates, voting requirements and Houston-area contacts

How to apply in Harris County

Start with the county’s election-worker application page.

Harris County tells applicants to wait until they have a confirmed vote-center placement before signing up for training. Without placement confirmation, the county says it cannot guarantee payment for the class.

The county also encourages applicants who speak and read Spanish, Vietnamese, or Chinese in addition to English for the class.

For the Nov. 3, 2026, election, Harris County’s dedicated training page says workers need one training class. Call 713-755-6965 to confirm which class meets the requirements and ask about remaining assignments.

Where to start in neighboring counties

  • Fort Bend – Fort Bend County provides election-worker application information online. Email the Elections Department at vote@fortbendcountytx.gov to confirm whether it is still accepting applicants for November.
  • Montgomery – Contact Montgomery County Elections at 936-539-7843 about placement. Its November training page says workers should not expect an early-voting assignment unless contacted by the office or an early-voting judge.
  • Brazoria – Use the county’s poll-worker application page. Ask the election office about remaining November assignments and training.
  • Galveston – Galveston County directs prospective election workers to its online Poll Worker Portal or to call 409-770-5108. Applicants interested in the Nov. 3 election should ask whether assignments remain available and confirm eligibility requirements, training dates, pay and expected working hours.

ALSO READ: Massive Texas backlog of voter registrations that scrambled workers has been cleared, state says

Do poll workers get paid?

Pay depends on the county and position.

Applicants should ask about their county’s current pay rate, training pay conditions, and expected payment schedule.

Can high school students work the polls?

Texas has a student election-clerk program for eligible students who are at least 16 on Election Day.

Requirements include U.S. citizenship, enrollment in a public, private, or qualified home school, required approval from a parent or guardian and the school, and completion of training. Student clerks are eligible for compensation.

Harris County’s student-worker page links to its application. The county recommends applying at least 60 days before Election Day, while noting there is no statutory deadline. Since the recommended lead time has passed, please contact the office about remaining opportunities.

What should you ask before accepting?

Ask the election office:

  • Are you still placing new workers for Nov. 3?
  • Which role and location would I be assigned?
  • What training must I complete?
  • What are the pay rate and training-pay conditions?
  • When do I show up, and how late could the assignment run?
  • Have you worked an election in the Houston area? Tell ENOUGH what a first-time applicant should know.

item.title: 2-alarm warehouse fire at UniClean America prompts hazmat response in northwest Houston
item.dc:creator: Katherine Levens
item.description: A 2-alarm fire heavily damaged the UniClean America warehouse on Antoine Drive in northwest Houston late Friday, spreading to nearby businesses and prompting a multi-department firefighting response.
item.content:encoded:
A 2-alarm fire tore through a warehouse at UniClean America on Antoine Drive in northwest Houston late Friday night, triggering a hazmat response and damaging several neighboring businesses.

The Northwest Fire Department responded around 8 p.m. to the 12100 block of Antoine, arriving to find the warehouse fully involved. UniClean America is a cleaning supply company, and the presence of chemicals on site added complexity to the firefighting effort.

Wind played a role in spreading the fire, and an estimated four to five businesses sustained at least smoke damage. No injuries were reported.

Multiple fire departments assisted at the scene. Crews ran a line to reach additional water sources as part of the firefighting effort.

  • Early voting starts Monday: What to bring, where to go and how to get help

Hazmat crews monitor runoff, air quality

With chemicals involved, hazmat crews responded to manage runoff from firefighting water and conduct air monitoring in the area. Booms were placed to help contain the runoff, and water testing showed a neutral pH level. Harris County Public Health was also called in to assist with runoff management.

Hazmat crews are still working to identify the specific products and chemicals that were stored at the facility.

Fire origin under investigation

The Harris County Fire Marshal’s Office is investigating the origin and cause of the fire. At this time, nothing suggests the fire was arson-related, though the investigation remains ongoing.

item.title: Harris County has 46 data centers and limited power to regulate them. Here’s what could change
item.dc:creator: Joy Addison, Austin McAfee
item.description: Harris County has 46 data centers, with at least six more in development. But as these facilities continue to expand, county leaders say they have limited power to regulate where they are built and how they affect nearby communities.
item.content:encoded:
Harris County has 46 data centers, with at least six more in development. But as these facilities continue to expand, county leaders say they have limited power to regulate where they are built and how they affect nearby communities.

During an Oct. 15 news conference, Harris County Attorney Abbie Kamin and Commissioner Lesley Briones outlined steps county leaders want to take to improve oversight and push state lawmakers for more local control.

What is a data center, and why are they a concern?

Data centers store and process digital information that powers everyday activities, including internet searches, streaming services and artificial intelligence.

But operating these facilities requires significant resources, especially electricity. Depending on their cooling systems, they can also use water and take up large amounts of land.

Dr. Ramanan Krishnamoorti, vice president for energy and innovation at the University of Houston, said electricity is the biggest resource data centers use. He also explained that these facilities need cooling systems to prevent computer equipment from overheating.

As more data centers are built, concerns include increased demand on the electric grid, water use, noise and potential effects on nearby neighborhoods.

During the news conference, Kamin said CenterPoint Energy expects to connect eight gigawatts of new data center demand in the Houston area by 2029, with about four additional gigawatts to follow. Kamin said that growth could increase peak electricity demand in the region by about 50%.

How can a data center be built without the county knowing?

One issue is that developers may be able to seek permits to build a data center without specifically identifying the project as one.

Krishnamoorti explained that developers can purchase land, apply for permits to construct a building and work directly with utility companies to arrange electricity service.

Because utility regulation largely happens at the state level, and Harris County does not have zoning authority, county officials may have limited involvement in where these facilities are built.

“Harris County is not permitted to regulate where they’re located through zoning,” Kamin said during the news conference.

Zoning rules generally determine how land can be used and where certain types of development can occur. Harris County does not have zoning authority, and the city of Houston also does not have traditional zoning.

Within incorporated cities, municipalities have their own land-use powers. In unincorporated areas, however, the county has limited authority to control where data centers are built specifically because they are data centers.

That does not mean data centers avoid all permits or regulations. They must still meet applicable requirements, which can include building plans, fire safety and utility connections. The issue is that the county has limited power to regulate their location.

What changes does Harris County want to make?

Commissioner Lesley Briones outlined steps county leaders want to take to improve oversight.

First, the county wants its Office of the County Engineer, Flood Control and Fire Marshal’s Office to notify commissioners when a major data center submits a traffic impact analysis, permit application or fire code plan review.

The goal is to give commissioners earlier notice of projects so they can better understand potential effects on nearby communities and determine what steps are possible under current law.

Second, the county wants its County Attorney’s Office to review what authority county officials already have over data center development.

Third, the county plans to work toward changes in state law that would give counties more oversight of data centers in unincorporated areas.

Briones said the county is studying how other counties and cities handle data center development to help determine what policies might work in Harris County.

According to Briones’ office, Harris County has not selected a specific regulatory model beyond these steps and its legislative advocacy.

Potential measures being discussed through the Conference of Urban Counties include requirements for closed-loop cooling systems, minimum distances between data centers and homes, and noise limits.

These are potential policy proposals, not rules Harris County has already adopted.

What happens next?

County officials want to work with other counties and state lawmakers ahead of the next legislative session, which begins in January 2027.

Briones said the county wants to protect residents and the environment while recognizing the potential economic benefits of data centers, including jobs and tax revenue.

The challenge is finding a balance between those benefits and concerns about electricity demand, water use, noise and neighborhood impacts.

For now, commissioners are seeking earlier notice of proposed projects and a clearer understanding of their legal authority. Any major expansion of the county’s regulatory powers would likely require action by state lawmakers.

item.title: Dayton ISD bus driver arrested after hit-and-run leaves 14-year-old boy fighting for his life
item.dc:creator: Brittany Taylor
item.description: A 70-year-old Dayton ISD bus driver has been arrested in connection with a hit-and-run that left a 14-year-old boy critically injured Friday morning, according to Dayton police.
item.content:encoded:
A 70-year-old Dayton ISD bus driver has been arrested in connection with a hit-and-run that left a 14-year-old boy critically injured Friday morning, according to Dayton police.

Ricky Eugene Cherry, a Dayton resident, was arrested following an investigation into the crash that happened between 6:15 and 6:30 a.m. Oct. 16 near U.S. Highway 90 eastbound and Stilson Road.

Police said the boy was struck by a vehicle whose driver left the scene without stopping to render aid.

The victim, identified by his family as Brantley, is being treated at Texas Children’s Hospital, where he is fighting for his life.

Brantley’s aunt contacted Grizzy’s Hood News to share information about her nephew, describing him as a bright, smart young boy. She said the family is devastated by what happened.

Police have not released the specific charges against Cherry or confirmed whether he was driving a school bus at the time of the crash.

The investigation remains ongoing.

Anyone with information about the incident is asked to contact the Dayton Police Department at 936-258-7621.

item.title: Cold morning temperatures move into Houston this weekend
item.dc:creator: Anthony Yanez
item.description: Morning temperatures will be the coldest since March
item.content:encoded:
Do you know what a cold front is? The number one comment I get when the winds change

Saturday’s forecast:

A wind advisory is in effect through 1:00 AM Saturday. With morning temperatures in the upper 40s and lower 50s, it will feel downright chilly, especially with the wind. The good news? Winds will ease Saturday afternoon, with highs climbing into the upper 60s and lower 70s.

Afternoon highs reach the upper 60s and lower 70s under mostly sunny skies. The Houston Cougars have a big game Saturday night against the Oklahoma State Cowboys at TDECU Stadium. The game should be a sellout. If you’re going, make sure you dress warm, temperatures fall from the 60s to the 50s.

Sunday’s forecast: Fall weather at its best!

If you love a cool, crisp fall day, Sunday is for you. We’ll start with temperatures in the 40s and 50s with calm winds before warming into the mid-70s in the afternoon. Expect mostly sunny skies, comfortable temperatures, and incredibly low humidity. It doesn’t get much better than this for a fall day in Houston.

Extended forecast:

Temperatures warm to the 80s on Tuesday with the humidity returning on Thursday. For now, I do not have a chance of rain in the next 10-days.

item.title: Why are Houston police the top searchers of the University of North Carolina's Flock network?
item.dc:creator: Bryce Newberry
item.description: Houston police are the number one searchers of a Flock camera network more than a thousand miles away, according to new data obtained by KPRC 2 News from the University of North Carolina at Charlotte.
item.content:encoded:
Houston police are the number one searchers of a Flock camera network more than a thousand miles away, according to new data obtained by KPRC 2 News from the University of North Carolina at Charlotte.

The automated license plate readers have gained a lot of attention in recent months over questions and concerns about privacy.

The data from March through May of this year shows the Houston Police Department ran 183,252 searches of the UNC Charlotte Flock network, which consists of 17 cameras.

“UNC Charlotte participates in Flock’s law enforcement network and shares limited search capability with participating law enforcement agencies that also share information with UNC Charlotte. For those agencies, a search can indicate whether a particular license plate was detected by a UNC Charlotte camera. The result provides the camera location, date and time. It does not provide the name of the person associated with the vehicle or its registration,” according to UNC’s website.

For context, the data shows HPD is the law enforcement agency with the highest amount of searches of UNC’s network, and it’s about five times more than searches conducted by the Texas Department of Public Safety.

“When an officer runs a license plate in Flock, the system searches a database of images that includes images from any camera shared with our department to identify a potential match,” the Houston Police Department told KPRC 2 News in a statement.

It’s part of a nationwide search feature offered by Flock, which the Pearland Police Department disabled last month.

According to a new report expected to be presented to the Pearland City Council next week, Pearland’s Flock network was searched 903,413 times by outside agencies from Aug. 10 through Sept. 9 this year, accounting for approximately 61 percent of the searches of Pearland’s network.

The nationwide search feature is reciprocal, meaning only agencies that participate are able to conduct a nationwide search.

With Pearland PD’s nationwide search feature turned off, Pearland officers are no longer able to conduct a nationwide search, but according to the city council report, PPD shares with 538 law enforcement agencies in Texas as part of a statewide search feature.

HPD told KPRC 2 News the department regularly reviews and investigates Flock usage by officers.

item.title: FBI Houston investigates suspicious mailings after white powder sent to Ted Cruz’s office
item.dc:creator: Brittany Taylor, Bryce Newberry
item.description: The FBI Houston field office is investigating at a federal building as authorities investigate a series of suspicious mailings sent to addresses nationwide, including an envelope containing white powder sent to Sen. Ted Cruz’s office.
item.content:encoded:
The FBI Houston field office is investigating at a downtown Houston federal building as authorities investigate a series of suspicious mailings sent to addresses nationwide.

The investigation is happening now at the Mickey Leland building on Smith Street.

An envelope containing a suspicious substance was sent to Sen. Ted Cruz’s office, according to a law enforcement source.

“I am grateful to law enforcement for their professionalism and to my dedicated team members, who work tirelessly on behalf of Texans,” Cruz said on X.

This afternoon, my Houston office received a suspicious piece of mail containing a white powder substance. The FBI, Houston Police and Fire Department, and U.S. Capitol Police responded swiftly.

I am grateful to law enforcement for their professionalism and to my dedicated team…

— Senator Ted Cruz (@SenTedCruz) October 16, 2026

The FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating the mailings, some of which contained an unknown substance, according to federal authorities.

The agencies are working with law enforcement partners to respond to each incident and identify the person or people responsible.

The suspicious letters were sent to various addresses across the country, including secretaries of state offices and their related election offices.

“The FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens,” the FBI said in a statement.

A source familiar tells KPRC 2 News everyone in the senator’s office is safe.

FBI is on scene at Sen. Ted Cruz's downtown Houston office after a law enforcement source tells me his office received an envelope containing a white powder, similar to other suspicious mailings nationwide. A source familiar says everyone in the senator's office is safe. @KPRC2 pic.twitter.com/1Ro9QnDUka

— KPRC 2 Bryce Newberry (@KPRC2Bryce) October 16, 2026

Authorities have not released additional details, citing the ongoing investigation.

KPRC 2’s reporter Sandy Torres and photographer Mike Lemons are outside the federal building in downtown Houston.

We will continue to follow this developing story and provide updates as more information becomes available.

item.title: Sisters Network INC. offers financial assistance, breast cancer resources for women in need
item.dc:creator: Paige Hubbard
item.description: Sisters Network Inc. provides financial assistance for screenings and treatment while raising awareness about breast cancer disparities affecting Black women
item.content:encoded:
As Breast Cancer Awareness Month highlights the importance of early detection, Sisters Network Inc. is working to help Black women overcome financial barriers to breast cancer screenings and treatment.

Caleen Allen, executive vice president of Sisters Network Inc., and Dee Manuel Cloud, a two-time breast cancer survivor and breast cancer recovery strategist, joined KPRC 2 to raise awareness about breast cancer disparities and highlight resources available to help women access screenings, treatment and financial assistance.

The Houston-based national organization provides emotional support, education and financial assistance through its network of more than 30 affiliate chapters across the country.

UNDERSTANDING THE ISSUE:

Caleen Allen points to medical research showing that Black women face higher breast cancer death rates and are more likely to be diagnosed with aggressive forms of the disease, including triple-negative breast cancer.

They also are more likely to be diagnosed at younger ages, highlighting the need for increased awareness and access to care.

Dee Manuel Cloud, president of the Sisters Network Greater Houston chapter, knows that reality firsthand. She was diagnosed with breast cancer at 35 and experienced a recurrence at 38.

“I am very passionate about making sure that women know the signs, what to look for during their monthly breast exams,” Cloud said.

Cloud said she discovered her own lump and encouraged women to pay attention to changes in their bodies and seek medical advice when something feels abnormal.

Symptoms can include a new lump, breast dimpling or abnormal nipple discharge. Persistent or unexplained changes also warrant medical attention, although they can have causes unrelated to cancer.

“I was fatigued all of a sudden. I was so tired all the time. I was nauseous all the time. But you know, we self-diagnose. Oh, that’s probably something I ate. Oh, I’m tired because I’ve been going nonstop. But it’s a different type of fatigue and is a different type of nausea. Like, don’t ignore those things,” she said.”

STANDING IN THE GAP FINANCIALLY:

Sisters Network also addresses the financial challenges that can accompany a diagnosis through its Karen E. Jackson Breast Cancer Assistance Program, established in 2006.

The program helps eligible survivors undergoing active treatment with expenses such as rent, mortgage payments and utilities. It also provides financial assistance for 3D mammograms to help women access screenings.

“Financial toxicity is real. Ladies need assistance, and not only just the financial side. You need help sometimes navigating with your insurance providers because sometimes that can be overwhelming for you. Your job. People lose their jobs because of going through treatment, and you need to know your rights,” said Allen.

The organization has distributed more than $2 million in financial assistance and mammogram resources through the program, according to Calleen Allen, executive vice president of Sisters Network Inc.

“When a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer, it is in no one’s budget,” Allen said, noting that treatment can bring additional expenses for medication, transportation and child care.

Cloud said she was fortunate to have two health insurance policies when she was diagnosed, but she has spoken with women who faced significant financial hardship.

“A breast cancer diagnosis can bankrupt you, and that’s just the reality of the situation,” she said.

Women seeking assistance can visit SistersNetworkInc.org and explore the resources available on the organization’s website. The American Cancer Society can also help patients identify financial assistance and other support services. Uninsured Harris County residents can explore care options through Harris Health.

Sisters Network is also hosts its annual National Black Breast Cancer Summit in Houston, bringing together survivors, medical experts and advocates to address disparities in breast cancer outcomes.

Allen said the organization wants women to know they do not have to navigate the experience alone.

“Sisters Network is there to walk hand in hand with any woman who needs assistance,” Allen said.

Both women emphasized the importance of making breast health a priority. Routine mammogram recommendations generally begin at age 40 for women at average risk, but those with a family history or other risk factors may need earlier screening based on guidance from their health care providers.

“Early detection is not a slogan,” Allen said. “It truly can save a woman’s life.”

item.title: Houston group says it’s delivered proof to the DA: Man ICE was hunting died years ago
item.dc:creator: Katherine Levens
item.description: A Houston immigration group, FIEL, says it obtained documentation proving ICE’s alleged target, identified as Jose Cervantes Mendoza, is actually Jose Hector Jimenez, who died in 2017.
item.content:encoded:
A Houston immigration advocacy group is calling out federal agents, presenting new evidence that the man ICE claimed to be searching for when their SUV struck Miguel Parra on October 10 had been dead for nearly a decade.

A Dead Man’s Photo on ICE’s Website

FIEL Houston executive director Cesar Espinosa announced this morning the organization has obtained documentation proving that Jose Cervantes Mendoza — the man ICE said agents were targeting — does not exist as a living person.

Espinosa says the man behind the alias was actually Jose Hector Jimenez, who died years ago attempting to re-enter the U.S. near Laredo — at the hands of U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

The story broke Wednesday when Jimenez’s daughter called FIEL’s office after seeing her late father’s photo on ICE’s website and in news coverage.

  • ICE officer placed on administrative leave after striking man with SUV in Houston

“She called our office sobbing because she saw her dad’s picture all over the news, all over the ICE website,” Espinosa said.

FIEL says it has turned that documentation over to the Harris County District Attorney’s office. The revelation aligns with a New York Times report published Thursday, which found ICE agents in Houston had been searching for a man whose family says died in 2017.

“Either immigration is starting to see ghosts, or they’re lying,” Espinosa said.

What Happened on October 10

ICE agents struck Miguel Parra with a government SUV during an enforcement operation in northwest Harris County. An ICE officer has since been placed on administrative leave.

A man identified only as Omar, who says he was with Parra that morning, appeared at Friday’s press conference to directly counter ICE’s claim that agents had visually identified a target before the vehicle struck Parra.

“I was with Miguel that day. He is my friend. He is also my boss. And that’s it, that’s all,” Omar said.

Parra’s Condition Is Getting Worse

Parra remains hospitalized with multiple fractures in his right leg and is facing reconstructive surgery on his ankle. Now, his mental health is deteriorating too.

His attorney, Kim Bruno, says Parra has fallen into depression after learning he may never have been near a legitimate enforcement target.

Making matters worse, Espinosa alleges Parra is surrounded around the clock by armed ICE agents — some allegedly present the day of the incident — who he says have been overheard mocking him.

“Joking, laughing, mocking him on the radio saying, ‘Oh, we’re gonna go get more families, we’re going to go get other people.’ And he’s hearing this 24-seven,” Espinosa said.

  • Handcuffed witness inside ICE SUV identified as family raises concerns about injured man’s hospital care

Key Witness Still Detained

Parra’s friend and witness Luis Enrique Delfin remains held at the Montgomery Processing Center. Attorney Bruno confirmed Delfin also sustained soft tissue injuries during the incident. His sister, Nidia Delfin, described a brother who is no longer himself.

“He is not the same guy that was out like last week. He is nervous, he is afraid,” she said.

FIEL is demanding Delfin’s immediate release so he can cooperate with the DA’s investigation without coercion.

FIEL’s Three Demands

  1. Release all ICE body camera footage from the morning of October 10.
  2. Free Luis Delfin so he can serve as an uncoerced witness in the DA’s investigation.
  3. Keep Miguel Parra in medical care until he has fully recovered — physically and mentally.

“At the end of the day, we seek transparency,” Espinosa said.

What’s Next

The Harris County District Attorney’s office is actively investigating. With FIEL delivering documentation of the alleged target’s death to prosecutors and an ICE officer already on administrative leave, pressure is growing on federal authorities to explain what really happened that morning.

ICE has not publicly responded to FIEL’s claims.

media:content.media:description: FIEL Houston executive director Cesar Espinosa.
